subject: passenger jet
title: What If a Jet Ran Out of Fuel at 41,000 Feet? In 1983 One Glided Home

scenes.text: What if a jet ran dry at 41,000 feet? In 1983 one did, over a unit mix-up.
July 23, 1983. An Air Canada 767 needs 22,300 kilograms of fuel. A conversion error loads 22,300 pounds: less than half.
Mid-flight, one engine starves, then the other. A jet with 69 people aboard is now a glider.
The captain happens to fly gliders. He has about 17 minutes, and one runway in reach: an old air base at Gimli.
It's now a drag strip, with cars and crowds on it that day. Coming in too high, he slips the jet sideways.
The nose gear collapses and the 767 grinds to a stop. Nobody dies. The plane was repaired and flew until 2008.

description:
What if a passenger jet ran out of fuel in mid-air? On 23 July 1983, Air Canada Flight 143, a Boeing 767 with 61 passengers and 8 crew, lost both engines at 41,000 feet after it was loaded with 22,300 pounds of fuel instead of 22,300 kilograms.
Captain Bob Pearson, a glider pilot, flew it for 17 minutes without power and used a forward slip to land on a former air base at Gimli, Manitoba, that had become a motorsport park. The nose gear collapsed, nobody was killed, and the aircraft flew until 2008.
